entries.title: [Editorial] A new era in neurology
entries.description: Neurological disorders are now the leading cause of disability worldwide, with profound consequences for patients, caregivers, and health-care systems. As populations age, the global burden of neurological disease will rise substantially. Yet neurology has transformed over the past two decades. Advances in genetics, molecular imaging, and biomarkers are shifting the field from being syndromic to biologically defined, reshaping disease management. Immunotherapies and gene-based approaches are beginning to modify the natural course of diseases previously thought untreatable.

entries.title: [Comment] Plasma biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease among middle-aged individuals
entries.description: Alzheimer's disease has a long preclinical phase in which neuropathological changes, such as amyloid β (Aβ) and tau pathology, accumulate over many years.1 This preclinical phase provides an opportunity for earlier disease detection and interventions to prevent or delay dementia. Emerging blood-based biomarkers provide a minimally invasive approach to assess Alzheimer's disease-related pathology and show promising diagnostic and prognostic value in symptomatic individuals.2 However, performance of these biomarkers in cognitively unimpaired, middle-aged populations remains unclear.

entries.title: [Comment] Prasinezumab: what have we learned from PASADENA and PADOVA?
entries.description: The concept of slowing down Parkinson's disease progression by using an antibody targeting aggregating forms of α-synuclein is intuitively very appealing. However, demonstrating efficacy of a potential disease-modifying therapy is highly challenging and a consensus has not been reached on the optimal trial design.1 The PASADENA trial evaluated two different doses of prasinezumab (an antibody that targets the C-terminal of aggregated forms of α-synuclein) given by monthly intravenous infusions in treatment-naive patients or those treated with monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) inhibitors.

entries.title: [Seminar] Alzheimer's disease
entries.description: Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and among the top ten leading causes of death in high-income countries. Exponential advances in epidemiology, genetics, diagnostic imaging and fluid biomarkers, treatment, and prevention in the last decade reinforce the notion that we are entering a new era in the clinical management of Alzheimer's disease. However, far from triumphalism, this momentum should be accelerated to achieve the goals of preventing Alzheimer's disease and arresting its progression.

entries.title: [Comment] Advancing tau-PET imaging in Alzheimer's disease
entries.description: The development of PET radioligands for the quantification of amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques over 20 years ago1 contributed substantially to Alzheimer's disease research, drug development, and clinical care. 10 years later, the development of radioligands for tau pathology,2 the second proteinopathy in Alzheimer's disease, has had a similar impact on Alzheimer's disease, becoming both an inclusion criterion and an outcome measure for recent Alzheimer's disease clinical trials.

entries.title: [Comment] Blood biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease: from detection to decisions
entries.description: Alzheimer's disease biomarkers have moved from being a focus of research to being used as clinical tools with remarkable speed. This shift is most visible in blood biomarkers, where advances in analytical and diagnostic accuracy now make detection of Alzheimer's pathology widely available to many patients. This progress should be recognised for what it is: a major gain for patients. Blood biomarkers can widen access and align diagnosis with the biology underlying the disease rather than syndromic labels alone.

entries.title: [Comment] Multi-arm multi-stage platform trials for neurological disease: accelerating progress
entries.description: Neurological diseases are the worldwide leading cause of ill health and disability.1 Although substantial progress has been made, such as modulating the inflammatory component of multiple sclerosis,2 neurodegenerative biology remains largely intractable, including in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and motor neuron disease. Recent scientific advances have deepened our understanding of neurodegenerative pathobiology, enabling targeted identification of mechanistically plausible candidate treatments.

As the stolen matter spirals inward, the system unleashes powerful radio waves and X-rays every 1.4 hours.

It will look deep into unexplored parts of the Milky Way, helping scientists compare planetary systems across very different galactic environments. The mission will also uncover rare Earth-sized planets, study thousands of exotic alien atmospheres, and provide a treasure trove of data that could reshape our understanding of how planets form.

entries.title: Hubble captures M88 on a perilous journey that could change it forever
entries.description: A stunning spiral galaxy called Messier 88 is racing through the crowded Virgo Cluster on a journey that will dramatically reshape its future. At its heart lies a supermassive black hole about 100 million times the mass of the Sun, while its graceful spiral arms sparkle with young star clusters and dark clouds of dust. But as M88 plunges deeper into the cluster over the next few hundred million years, powerful forces will strip away much of the gas it needs to create new stars.

Using a cutting-edge sensor system that tracked piano key movements at 1,000 frames per second, researchers discovered that elite pianists subtly manipulate keys in ways that listeners can genuinely hear, even if they’ve never played piano before.
